1.about: A bold, orchestrally conceived sonata whose hammering opening theme openly recalls Beethoven’s ‘Hammerklavier’ Sonata. The slow movement is a set of variations on an old German folk song, ‘Verstohlen geht der Mond auf’, and the fiery finale recasts the first movement’s theme in a galloping 9/8.
1.ctx: Although numbered Op. 1, it was finished after the F-sharp minor Sonata. Brahms chose it to introduce himself to the world: he played it to Robert and Clara Schumann in Düsseldorf in 1853, and Schumann’s famous article ‘Neue Bahnen’ (‘New Paths’) hailed the twenty-year-old as the coming genius of German music. Clara found the whole ‘full of exuberant fantasy, intimacy of expression and mastery of form’.
parts: A heroic, Beethovenian opening built from a hammered, rising theme.
Variations on the folk song ‘Verstohlen geht der Mond auf’, the earliest-dated part of the sonata (April 1852).
Scherzo: Allegro molto e con fuoco
A driving, fiery scherzo with a broader trio in C major.
A galloping rondo that transforms the first movement’s theme.
facts: Numbered Op. 1 although the F-sharp minor Sonata was written first.
Its opening deliberately echoes Beethoven’s ‘Hammerklavier’ Sonata.
Brahms played it to the Schumanns in 1853, the meeting that made his name.
Henle rates it level 8 (ABRSM FRSM).

2.about: The most turbulent of the three sonatas, full of wild, dramatic contrasts. The slow movement is a set of variations on an old German song, and the scherzo is built from the same theme, so the two central movements grow from a single idea. The finale opens with a free, rhapsodic introduction before a restless Allegro.
2.ctx: Completed in November 1852, this was the first of Brahms’s three sonatas to be written, though published second. He dedicated it to Clara Schumann, and Robert Schumann wrote to him that ‘your second sonata, my friend, has brought me much closer to you’.
parts: A stormy, tightly argued opening full of explosive octaves.
Variations on an old German song, intimate and inward.
A scherzo built from the slow movement’s theme, with a lyrical trio.
Finale: Introduzione (Sostenuto) – Allegro non troppo e rubato
A rhapsodic introduction leads to a passionate, restless finale.
facts: The first of Brahms’s sonatas to be completed.
Dedicated to Clara Schumann.
The slow movement and scherzo share the same theme.
Henle rates it level 8 (ABRSM FRSM).

5.about: Brahms’s last and largest sonata, in five movements rather than four. A massive, orchestral first movement is followed by a rapt slow movement headed by lines of a love poem by C. O. Sternau, a vigorous scherzo, a sombre Intermezzo titled ‘Rückblick’ (‘Looking back’) that recalls the slow movement in funereal colours, and a finale that ends in triumph.
5.ctx: Much of the sonata is closely connected to Brahms’s visit to Robert and Clara Schumann in Düsseldorf in autumn 1853, and it may have been inspired by Schumann’s own F-minor Sonata, Op. 14. The critic Eduard Hanslick wrote that ‘the whole of Brahms is here, though still under the spell of Schumann’. After it, Brahms wrote no further piano sonatas.
parts: A grand, symphonic opening of huge chords and sweeping contrasts.
A love song headed by lines from Sternau’s poem, ending in a radiant D-flat major.
A swaggering waltz-scherzo with a chorale-like trio.
‘Looking back’: the slow movement’s theme returns as a muffled funeral march.
A rondo that builds to a jubilant coda in F major.
facts: Written in five movements rather than the usual four.
The slow movement is headed by lines of a poem by C. O. Sternau.
His last piano sonata — he never wrote another.
Henle rates it level 9 (ABRSM FRSM).

4.about: A fiery, dark scherzo with two contrasting trios, written when Brahms was eighteen. Its driving rhythms and dense textures show the influence of Chopin’s scherzos and of Beethoven.
4.ctx: Brahms’s earliest surviving piano work. It particularly delighted Robert Schumann, who drew public attention to the young composer in his 1853 article ‘Neue Bahnen’.
facts: His earliest surviving piano work.
Written at eighteen, in 1851.
Henle rates it level 7.

9.about: Sixteen variations on a melancholy theme from Robert Schumann’s Bunte Blätter, Op. 99. The variations are intimate rather than showy, full of canons and allusions, and one quotes a theme by Clara Schumann herself.
9.ctx: Written in Düsseldorf in 1854, soon after Robert Schumann was admitted to the asylum at Endenich, when Brahms stayed near Clara to support the family. Clara had written her own variations on the same theme, and the two sets form a musical conversation between them.
facts: The theme comes from Schumann’s Bunte Blätter, Op. 99.
Clara Schumann wrote her own variations on the same theme.
Henle rates it level 7.

21/1.about: Eleven variations on a calm, hymn-like theme of Brahms’s own in D major. The set is lyrical and inward, with a long, hushed final variation over a trilled pedal.
21/1.ctx: Published in 1862 together with the Variations on a Hungarian Song as Op. 21. Clara Schumann admired the set’s quiet depth.
facts: Published as a pair with the Hungarian Song variations.
The theme is Brahms’s own.
Henle rates it level 7 (ABRSM FRSM recommended).

21/2.about: Thirteen short, energetic variations on a Hungarian tune whose bars alternate between 3/4 and 4/4 time, ending in a brilliant finale.
21/2.ctx: Brahms’s love of Hungarian music dates from his early tours with the Hungarian violinist Ede Reményi in 1853. The set was published with the Variations on an Original Theme as Op. 21.
facts: The theme alternates bars of 3/4 and 4/4.
Reflects his early tours with violinist Ede Reményi.
Henle rates it level 7.

24.about: Twenty-five variations and a monumental fugue on the Air from a harpsichord suite in B-flat major by Handel. The variations range from Baroque-style ornament to a siciliano, a musette and a thunderous march, before the fugue builds to one of the grandest endings in the piano repertoire.
24.ctx: Written in September 1861 as a birthday present for Clara Schumann, who gave its first performance. After hearing Brahms play it, Richard Wagner remarked that it showed what could still be done with the old forms in the hands of someone who knew how to use them.
facts: Written as a birthday gift for Clara Schumann.
The theme is the Air from Handel’s Suite in B-flat major, HWV 434.
Ends with a large-scale fugue.
Henle rates it level 9 (ABRSM FRSM recommended).

35.about: Two books of fourteen variations each on Paganini’s famous 24th Caprice. Brahms subtitled the work ‘Studies for the Pianoforte’: each variation tackles a specific technical problem — sixths, octaves, leaps, cross-rhythms, glissandi — making it one of the most demanding works in the repertoire.
35.ctx: Composed soon after Brahms settled in Vienna and associated with the virtuoso pianist Carl Tausig. Liszt and later Rachmaninoff also wrote famous works on the same Paganini theme.
facts: Brahms called it ‘Studies for the Pianoforte’.
Two books of fourteen variations each.
The theme is Paganini’s Caprice No. 24.
Henle rates it level 9 (ABRSM FRSM recommended).

18.about: Brahms’s own piano arrangement of the variation movement of his String Sextet No. 1, Op. 18: a stern, archaic D-minor theme followed by six variations that move from sombre counterpoint to warm D-major lyricism.
18.ctx: Brahms made the arrangement in 1860 for Clara Schumann’s birthday. Henle includes it as an appendix to its edition of the piano variations.
facts: Made as a birthday present for Clara Schumann.
Arranged from the String Sextet No. 1, Op. 18.
Henle rates it level 6.

10.about: Four ballades that move from dark narrative to quiet introspection. The first is inspired by the grim Scottish ballad ‘Edward’, a dialogue between a mother and her son who has killed his father; the others are pure character pieces, ending with the long, dreamy B-major Ballade.
10.ctx: Written in 1854, the year of Robert Schumann’s breakdown, while Brahms was close to the Schumann family in Düsseldorf. Brahms told Clara they were ‘not very difficult, and even less difficult to understand’.
parts: A stark narrative after the Scottish ballad ‘Edward’, with a violent central climax.
A gentle opening that gives way to agitated and scherzando episodes.
A spiky, demonic scherzo with an ethereal, bell-like trio.
A long, dreamy close with an inward central section in B minor.
facts: No. 1 is based on the Scottish ballad ‘Edward’, from Herder’s Stimmen der Völker.
Brahms called them ‘not very difficult’.
Henle rates the set at levels 6–7.

39.about: Sixteen short waltzes in the spirit of Schubert’s Ländler, more intimate than Viennese ballroom music. They move through a carefully planned sequence of keys and moods, and No. 15 in A-flat has become one of Brahms’s most famous melodies.
39.ctx: Originally written for piano four hands and published in 1866. His publisher persuaded Brahms to make a solo version, and he produced two: a demanding one ‘for clever hands’ and a simplified one ‘perhaps for the more beautiful ones’. This entry and its levels follow the demanding solo version.
parts: A wistful waltz with a darker colouring.
A waltz with a Hungarian-flavoured melancholy.
The famous one: a gently rocking melody among Brahms’s best-known ideas.
A quiet, wistful close to the set.
facts: Originally for piano four hands.
Brahms made two solo versions, one of them simplified.
Dedicated to the critic Eduard Hanslick.
Henle rates the solo waltzes at levels 5–7.

76.about: Brahms’s first collection of short piano pieces, alternating restless capriccios with more lyrical intermezzi — the two genres that would dominate his late piano music.
76.ctx: The first Capriccio was written in 1871 as a gift for Clara Schumann; the rest followed mostly in 1878. The set was published in two books in 1879.
parts: A surging capriccio of dark, rolling arpeggios, first written for Clara Schumann.
A light, staccato capriccio, one of Brahms’s most popular short pieces.
A delicate, music-box-like piece of syncopated melody.
Capriccio: Agitato, ma non troppo presto
A turbulent capriccio full of cross-rhythms.
A lyrical intermezzo built on duplets against triplets.
A simple, archaic-sounding piece framing a warmer centre.
Capriccio: Grazioso ed un poco vivace
A playful, swirling close to the set.
facts: His first published set of short piano pieces.
No. 1 was written for Clara Schumann in 1871.
Henle rates the pieces at levels 5–7.

79.about: Two large, passionate pieces in sonata-like forms. The B-minor Rhapsody alternates stormy outer sections with a hushed, dreamlike trio; the G-minor Rhapsody drives forward with relentless energy and tonal instability.
79.ctx: Written in the summer of 1879 at Pörtschach on the Wörthersee, a productive period that also produced the Violin Concerto and the Violin Sonata No. 1. The pieces were dedicated to the pianist Elisabeth von Herzogenberg.
parts: Stormy outer sections framing a mysterious, murmuring trio in B major.
Molto passionato, ma non troppo allegro
A relentless, tonally restless piece in compact sonata form.
facts: Dedicated to Elisabeth von Herzogenberg.
Written at Pörtschach in 1879.
Henle rates them levels 7 and 6.

116.about: Seven pieces that play off three passionate capriccios against four dreamy intermezzi, forming a loosely connected cycle framed by two D-minor capriccios.
116.ctx: Written in the summer of 1892 at Bad Ischl alongside the Intermezzi Op. 117. They open the great series of late piano pieces (Opp. 116–119) that Brahms wrote in 1892–93.
parts: A fierce, driving opening full of cross-rhythms.
A melancholy intermezzo with a flowing central section.
A passionate capriccio framing a noble E-flat centre.
Intermezzo: Andante con grazia ed intimissimo sentimento
A strange, halting piece of offbeat sighs.
A stormy close returning to the key of the opening.
facts: Opens Brahms’s late series of piano pieces, Opp. 116–119.
Three capriccios alternate with four intermezzi.
Henle rates the pieces at levels 5–7.

117.about: Three quiet, deeply introspective intermezzi. The first is a lullaby headed by lines from a Scottish ballad in Herder’s translation; the second flows in delicate arpeggios; the third is a dark, bare-octave piece in C-sharp minor.
117.ctx: Written in summer 1892 at Bad Ischl. Brahms described them as ‘three lullabies of my sorrows’, and Clara Schumann wrote that in these pieces she at last felt musical life stir once again in her soul.
parts: A lullaby headed by lines from the Scottish ‘Lady Anne Bothwell’s Lament’.
Andante non troppo e con molto espressione
Flowing, sighing arpeggios of great intimacy.
A sombre melody in bare octaves, with a more luminous centre.
facts: Brahms called them ‘lullabies of my sorrows’.
No. 1 quotes a Scottish lullaby in Herder’s German translation.
Henle rates them levels 5–6.

118.about: Six pieces of great variety: a passionate opening intermezzo, the famous A-major Intermezzo, a heroic Ballade, a canonic F-minor intermezzo, the serene F-major Romanze and a haunting E-flat minor close built on a Dies irae-like theme.
118.ctx: Written in summer 1893 at Bad Ischl and dedicated to Clara Schumann, who said the pieces contained ‘a wealth of sentiment in the smallest of dimensions’. The set was Brahms’s penultimate piano opus.
parts: Intermezzo: Allegro non assai, ma molto appassionato
A short, surging piece that begins off the tonic.
The beloved A-major Intermezzo, one of Brahms’s best-known pieces.
A heroic ballade with a gentle B-major centre.
A restless piece built on strict canon between the hands.
A serene pastoral with a decorated central section in D major.
A desolate close on a theme reminiscent of the Dies irae.
facts: Dedicated to Clara Schumann.
Contains the famous Intermezzo in A major and the Romanze in F major.
Henle rates the pieces at levels 6–7.

119.about: Brahms’s last work for solo piano: three contrasting intermezzi — a slow cascade of falling thirds, a restless E-minor waltz and a playful C-major piece — followed by the grand E-flat Rhapsody, which unexpectedly ends in E-flat minor.
119.ctx: Written in 1893 at Bad Ischl. After these pieces Brahms wrote no more solo piano music. The Rhapsody’s opening sustains five-bar phrases for sixty bars.
parts: A slow, hovering piece of falling thirds and dissonances.
A nervous opening that turns into a graceful waltz in the middle.
A light, humorous piece with the melody in the inner voice.
A heroic march-like rhapsody that ends, unusually, in E-flat minor.
facts: His last work for solo piano.
The Rhapsody ends in the minor, not the major.
Henle rates the pieces at levels 6–8.

WoO1.about: Brahms’s own solo-piano arrangements of the first ten of his 21 Hungarian Dances. They are settings of popular Hungarian and Roma-style melodies, and the solo versions are considerably harder than the original duets.
WoO1.ctx: Brahms offered the dances to his publisher without an opus number, stressing that he had only ‘set’ existing melodies rather than composed them. They became some of his most successful music, and the solo arrangement of Nos. 1–10 appeared in 1872.
parts: A passionate dance, among the most popular of the set.
A fiery dance alternating tension and release.
A graceful, lighter dance in F major.
A long, brooding dance with a quick central section.
The world-famous dance, based on a csárdás by Béla Kéler.
A capricious dance of sudden tempo changes.
facts: Published without opus number because Brahms regarded them as arrangements.
Originally for piano four hands.
No. 5 is based on a csárdás by Béla Kéler.
Henle rates the solo versions at levels 7–8.
